messages:
ian_support: FYI got an escalation from @customer_ops — their Private control plane mTLS started failing right after they enabled a Palo Alto SSL Forward Proxy policy.  Error: repeated handshake failures.

customer_ops: Yes, we flipped the 'decrypt forward-proxy' rule last night to inspect egress TLS. After that our services that use client certs to talk to private-control.redwood.ai:8443 started failing.

sara_sre: Can you paste the client-side error you see? Also which client (curl/java/golang) and which cert/key format?

customer_ops: Go HTTP client inside their microservice. Error in logs: `tls: handshake failure` and on retry we see `tls: client certificate required`. We supplied certs.

devin_neteng: Likely SSL Forward Proxy is terminating the TLS and re-issuing a server cert — that will break mutual TLS because the Palo Alto is not forwarding the client cert. Common with forward-proxy decryption. Can you confirm if the FW is doing true passthrough or MITM?

customer_ops: The policy is explicitly set to Decrypt (Forward Proxy). They wanted to inspect outbound TLS. They said the device performs on-the-fly certs signed by their internal CA.

ian_support: That matches. mTLS requires end-to-end client cert validation. If the proxy terminates TLS, the control plane will never see the client cert. For Private control plane we require TLS peer auth — cannot accept proxied client certs.

customer_ops: Is there a recommended config? We can't disable inspection broadly.

devin_neteng: Two paths: 1) Configure a policy exception for the control plane FQDN `private-control.redwood.ai` (and the IP ranges Redwood provided) to do ssl-pass-through / no-decrypt so the TLS is end-to-end. 2) If pass-through isn't possible, configure the firewall to forward the client cert via header injection is not viable for mTLS. We must do passthrough.

sara_sre: Also check SNI rewriting rules — if the proxy rewrites SNI to an internal hostname the control plane will reject. tcpdump of the ClientHello will show SNI and whether it's rewritten.

ian_support: Repro steps we asked customer to run and attach: 
```
# capture just the 3-way + TLS handshake to file
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -s 0 -w /tmp/mtls_issue.pcap host 203.0.113.45 and port 8443
# quick TLS client check (use local cert/key used by service)
openssl s_client -connect private-control.redwood.ai:8443 -cert client.pem -key client.key -showcerts -state -tlsextdebug
```

customer_ops: Attached `openssl` output snippet: `---
CONNECTED(00000003)
SSL_connect:ssl3_read_bytes:tlsv1 alert unknown ca
140735388361344:error:14094410:SSL routines:ssl3_read_bytes:tlsv1 alert unknown ca:../ssl/record/rec_layer_s3.c:1524:---`

devin_neteng: That `unknown ca` suggests the firewall's re-signed server cert chain is not trusted by your client (or it changed SNI). But the bigger issue is the proxy is terminating the upstream TLS so the control plane never receives the client cert.

customer_ops: We verified via tcpdump that the ClientHello leaving the service goes to the Palo Alto, and the packet toward Redwood shows a different server cert chain issued by internal-CA.

ian_support: Outcome / recommended remediation: Add an allowlist rule for the control plane host/IPs to bypass TLS decryption for egress to `private-control.redwood.ai:8443`. If they insist on inspection, they need to implement a transparent TCP passthrough for that route.

customer_ops: We'll request an exception for the control plane FQDN and test. Thanks.

deploy-bot: NOTE: private-control.redwood.ai IP ranges used on the Private plane (for customer's region) were posted to the account's firewall guide last week — confirm with account docs before making broad allowlist.

sara_sre: If they still see failures after the passthrough rule, ask for: 1) pcap of the failed handshake, 2) `openssl s_client -debug` output, 3) local service's TLS config (cert format, cipher list). We'll help correlate. :thumbsup:

ian_support: Closing loop here once customer confirms pass-through fixes it. If not, we'll escalate to eng-runtime with packet capture and our control plane TLS logs.
